## Changes

### Installer runs Dafny and Boogie on hosts with only .NET 10

[`d92473f1f023`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/d92473f1f023fc1599bc171d0c15f1daa0a777d2) · [log `584c77f06146`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/353e094e-5bc2-42ab-966c-b858752c38d6/584c77f06146c3e893761af0bedfc3c6c7abc1b6642bb2538f8281b9a0dbed78.jsonl.gz)

On Ubuntu 26.04 only the .NET 10 runtime is packaged, and Boogie (built for .NET 8) refuses to start. When no .NET 8 runtime is present, install.sh now writes launchers for dafny and boogie into ~/.local/bin, ahead of ~/.dotnet/tools on PATH, that set DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD=Major. gh_asset also now prints nothing (rather than the string "null") when no release asset matches, so a fallback written as $(a || b) receives only the other URL. Verified on a fresh Ubuntu 26.04.1 VM with only Microsoft.NETCore.App 10.0.14: bash -n passes, dafny --version reports 4.11.0 and boogie starts through the launcher, and the new jq filter returns the first matching URL or exits 4 with no output on a sample release JSON.

### Verification report names the machine of every result and calibrates estimates per machine

change `spvvulkrmxtn` · [log `dc30323604eb`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/353e094e-5bc2-42ab-966c-b858752c38d6/dc30323604ebe5941eb48b23aaf539bdb4599a7c90978fbdefff902f23e1e58f.jsonl.gz)

Results already recorded their host and environment, but the Markdown report showed neither and pooled every machine into one calibration table. Until now every result came from one 8-core aarch64 WSL2 laptop (FilSurface); the queue is now running on claude-vm, a 28-vCPU x86_64 VM, so durations from the two would mix. report now labels each result with its machine (host, architecture, WSL, CPUs), the JSON report gains a machine field per result and a calibrationByHost table (calibration keeps its old pooled shape), and the Markdown report prints one calibration table per machine. verification/README.md records which machine ran which results and no longer calls the WSL laptop 'this machine'. Verified with the pipeline's unit tests (22 pass, one extended to check the label and the per-host table) and by rendering the report over the 88 collected results.

### 2. 2026-11-06 16:57 UTC

> This is all working as designed, we may upgrade setup later but for now the missing capabilities are not needed. Let's try to publish Cloudflare logs next (unless this happened as part of push, then do nothing). After that, let's review run-verification -- I would like to run all the verification jobs on this machine. Its config designed for a much weaker system. Ensure that Claude Code has a good amount of memory for loops (like 8GB, in case experiments are run), then you can dedicate whatever else VM does not need to running verification jobs more efficiently.

**Reply:**

The runner picked up the new budget: 12 workers, 24 CPUs, 32 GiB, at most 14 GiB per job, each step capped in its own systemd scope. Only 5 jobs started at first. That's because a job that needs a fresh jvmcontract build reserves the 6 GiB build allowance instead of its own memory limit. Once the builds are cached, more jobs can run at once.

**What I did:**
- **Cloudflare logs:** nothing needed. The earlier push had already uploaded them, and `check --remote` confirms every log is live on the CDN with 0 errors.
- **8 GB for Claude Code loops:** I added `export FEATURE_LOOP_MEMORY_MAX=8G` to `~/.profile`. It applies to new login shells, so start any loop from a new SSH session, or prefix the command with `FEATURE_LOOP_MEMORY_MAX=8G`. Only one feature loop can run at a time, because it always uses the same systemd scope name.
- **Runner budget** (`verification/pipeline.local.toml`, which is machine-local and not committed): the existing file allowed 6 workers, 22 CPUs and 30G. I raised it to 12 workers, 24 CPUs and 32G. Of the 46 GiB, that leaves 8G for a loop, about 2G for the OS, Docker and interactive sessions, and about 4G spare, since the VM has no swap. Jobs ask for only 1–2 CPUs each, so the old worker count, not memory, was holding the runner back. I also corrected that file's comment, which wrongly said up to four loops could run at once.
